The selectable variable is not speed, abundance, GC, wobble, or folding; it is the expected cost of rare wrong protein products.

The mechanism would be this. At a given Ser site, the intended product is identical whether the codon is UCN or AGY. But the wrong products are not identical. UCN codons have one-step neighbors leading into amino acids such as Pro, Ala, Thr, Phe, Tyr, Cys, Leu, Trp, and for UCA/UCG, Stop. AGY codons have a different neighborhood, including Arg, Gly, Asn, Thr, Ile, and Cys. Therefore, a synonymous UCN↔AGY choice can change the distribution of mistranslated peptides while leaving the intended amino-acid sequence unchanged.
That becomes a plausible expression-level pressure because highly expressed proteins generate many translation events. Even a rare codon-specific error can create many aberrant molecules if the gene is highly translated. Selection need not care about the average codon speed; it can care about whether the rare error product is toxic, aggregation-prone, dominant-negative, catalytically misleading, or disruptive at a conserved site. The relevant quantity is something like:

$$\text{cost}(c,s,\sigma)
=
E_g \sum_{n\in N_1(c)}
p(n\mid c,\sigma)\cdot D_s(\mathrm{AA}(n),\mathrm{Ser}),$$

where  $c$  is the Ser codon,  $s$  is the protein site,  $\sigma$  is the cellular condition,  $E_g$  is expression/translation burden,  $p(n\mid c,\sigma)$  is the condition-specific probability of a one-step decoding or aminoacylation error, and  $D_s$  is the site-specific damage caused by inserting the wrong amino acid. The Ser split matters because UCN and AGY have different  $N_1(c)$  neighborhoods. The code’s missing Hamming-1 bridge becomes biologically meaningful only if this error-cost term is real.
The best molecular substrate for this is conditional Ser-tRNA channel fidelity, not ordinary tRNA supply. Ser codons are decoded through different Ser-tRNA isoacceptor routes. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases do not recognize tRNAs only through anticodons; tRNA identity can involve overall structure and non-anticodon features, and synthetases can also have editing functions that affect charging fidelity. 维基百科 That creates room for UCN- and AGY-decoding Ser-tRNA channels to differ in aminoacylation kinetics, mischarging susceptibility, EF-Tu/EF1A acceptance, or near-cognate rejection even after controlling for how much tRNA is present.
There is also precedent for synonymous codon degeneracy being conditionally lifted. Subramaniam, Pan, and Cluzel reported in E. coli that amino-acid perturbations can split synonymous codons into robust and sensitive classes, with protein-synthesis differences up to roughly hundred-fold; they reported that the hierarchy was not explained by usual tRNA abundance or codon-usage rules, but by competition among tRNA isoacceptors for aminoacylation. arXiv For the present claim, that result is only a scaffold, not proof. If the Ser effect is merely “one island has more charged tRNA,” it is disqualified as tRNA supply. The stronger surviving version is: at matched charged-tRNA availability and matched dwell, UCN and AGY produce different rare wrong-amino-acid spectra or different wrong-product costs.
The most convincing biological story is therefore not “AGY is slow” or “UCN is abundant.” It is:
A Ser residue has two synonymous codon islands available. Under ordinary conditions, both usually yield Ser. Under stress, limitation, proteostasis load, altered SerRS behavior, or tRNA-modification stress, the two islands differ in fidelity failure mode. One island may be more prone to near-cognate Arg/Gly/Asn/Ile-type errors; the other may be more exposed to Pro/Ala/Leu/Stop/Trp-type errors. Highly expressed genes, or highly constrained Ser residues, preferentially use the island whose error spectrum is less damaging at that site. The split is then not a general “better codon” axis but a site-conditional error-spectrum axis.
The decisive confounders are harsh.
First, charged-tRNA supply in disguise. Measuring lower output from AGY or UCN under serine stress is not enough. That could be uncharged tRNA abundance, tAI, gene copy, aminoacylated fraction, or ordinary codon optimality. The mechanism survives only if the UCN/AGY difference remains after charged Ser-tRNA availability is equalized or explicitly accounted for.
Second, wobble in disguise. UCN and AGY are decoded by different anticodon systems, so any effect caused by wobble pairing breadth or position-34 modification is not the desired mechanism. The relevant residual signal must come from wrong-product identity, charging/proofreading, tRNA-body features, or near-cognate competition not reducible to wobble class.
Third, ribosome dwell masquerading as fidelity. A reporter can show lower fluorescence because translation is slower, ribosomes collide, elongation pauses, or drop-off increases. That would not establish the proposed mechanism. The decisive readout is peptide-resolved mistranslation: which wrong amino acids appear at the Ser site, at what rate, and under what condition.
Fourth, sequence-composition confounding. UCN and AGY differ in GC, purine/pyrimidine content, CpG/UpA potential, local RNA structure, splice/regulatory motifs, and codon-pair context. A natural-genome enrichment of one island over the other is nearly uninterpretable unless those are removed.
Fifth, Stop leakage from the Stop/Ser decomposition. UCA and UCG are one mutation or misread away from UAA/UAG-like Stop outcomes, while UCU/UCC are not. If the entire effect is really UCA/UCG avoidance, then it is a Stop-adjacency mechanism, not a Ser-split mechanism. A true sense-side Ser split effect must distinguish UCN-as-island from AGY-as-island without collapsing into UCA/UCG-specific nonsense risk.
Sixth, protein-position confounding. Ser codon usage may correlate with phosphorylation motifs, disorder, low-complexity regions, catalytic Ser, transmembrane boundaries, secretion signals, or taxon-specific gene classes. That could produce a real biological signal but not the proposed translation-level mechanism. The mechanism survives only if the same Ser residue, in matched context, changes its measured error spectrum or error cost when recoded between UCN and AGY.
So the strongest possible claim is narrow: the Ser split could align with selection if organisms exploit UCN and AGY as two synonymous fidelity modes, choosing between different rare-error spectra at highly expressed or functionally sensitive Ser sites. That is the cleanest mechanism because it is the only one that makes the missing Hamming-1 bridge itself relevant. Supply, wobble, GC, codon pairs, mRNA stability, and dwell can all explain codon choice without caring about the Ser graph defect. Error-spectrum selection directly cares about the Hamming-1 neighborhood.
If this route survives, the sharpest next question is: At matched Ser sites and matched expression context, does UCN↔AGY recoding change the peptide-resolved mistranslation spectrum in the direction predicted by the natural codon choice at highly expressed, functionally constrained Ser residues?
